dedupe_keys.name: cascading effects of the 2018 rhine low water on inland shipping supply chains

description: This study examines how the severe low discharge of the Rhine in 2018 cascaded through inland waterway transport into supply chains, and proposes a way to include such effects in climate risk assessment. Frederik Vinke, Mark van Koningsveld and co-authors from Delft University of Technology, Deltares and Rijkswaterstaat published it in Climate Risk Management in 2022. In 2018 the reduced water depth cut the river's transport capacity for several months and caused shortages of raw materials and fuels far inland; the growing share of larger vessels has made supply via the Rhine more sensitive to low depths, and climate change may make such droughts more frequent. Because no integral model linked the state of the river to supply chain performance at corridor scale, the authors present a method that explicitly includes cascading effects of low discharge and of mitigation measures at system level, and show that it can describe effects and risks for fleet management and terminal operation. Coverage: the Rhine and the Rhine-Alpine corridor, with the 2018 event as reference. Access: open-access article. Licence and cost: CC BY 4.0, free. Caveats: a method paper with an illustrative application, and input data are not released with it. It supports climate adaptation, network flow and resilience studies of waterborne freight. It relates to the CCNR Act now paper, the UNCHAIN Mannheim low water case study and the OpenTNSim model in the catalogue.
